Robots usually slow down for canning to detect objects while moving. Additionally, the robot’s camera is configured with a low framerate to track the velocity of the detection algorithms. This would be constrained while executing tasks and exploring, making robots increase the task execution time. AMD has developed the Vitis-AI framework to deploy detection algorithms into field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). However, this tool does not fully use the FPGAs’ programmable logic (PL). In this work, we use the FINN architecture to deploy three artificial neural networks (ANNs), mobile neural network (MobileNet) v1 with 4-bit quantisation, convolutional neural network (CNV) with 2-bit quantisation, and CNV with 1-bit quantisation (bynary neural network (BNN)), inside a FPGA’s PL. The models were trained on the red grape chunk classification (RG2C) dataset. This is a self-acquired dataset released in open access. MobileNet v1 performed better, reaching a success rate of 98 % and a speed of inference of 6611 FPS. In this work, we proved that we can use FPGAs to speed up ANNs and make them suitable for attention mechanisms.
Index Terms—edge computing, binary neural network (BNN), FPGA, FINN, MobileNet, convolutional neural vector (CNV), computer vision

The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) is posing significant computing challenges. These algorithms demand high computing power, usually delivered to a power-consuming graphical processing units (GPUs). This aspect poses significant challenges while computing in mobile robots, when they cannot access external services.

Heterogeneous computing is the integration of diverse processor systems to address a specific scientific computing challenge. Such platforms consist of a variety of computational units and technologies, including multi-core computer processing units (CPUs), GPUs, and FPGAs. These components offer flexibility and adaptability for a broad spectrum of application domains [1]. These computational units can significantly boost the overall system efficiency and decrease power consumption by parallelising tasks that demand extensive CPU resources over prolonged periods.

Accelerators, such as GPUs and FPGAs, are designed for massively parallel processing. Namely, GPUs are designed for conducting matrix multiplications. However, convolution neural networks (CNNs) are inherently parallel but unsuitable for matrix representation. Application-specific integrated circuits

(ASICs) are customised designs of FPGAs, aimed at promising and specifying operation executions. When designed for processing CNNs, ASICs can match the speed of FPGAs.

CNNs are the most common type of ANNs for visual recognition and identification. Several researchers have explored efficient types of CNNs to address the challenges of detecting objects in near real-time. Notable examples include Tiny- YOLO [2], [3], YOLACT [4] or other innovative solutions [5]–[7]. However, in embedded GPUs, these ANNs are not fast enough yet. Other solutions designed for computation in near real-time in embedded devices are FPGAs, TensorFlow processing units (TPUs), Intel neural computing sticks (NCSs), and other dedicated ASICs [8]. In these devices, quantising the ANNs for efficient computation [9] is common. Magalh˜aes, S.C., et al. [10] made a deep benchmark on several different devices and concluded the benefits of using FPGAs for computing deep learnings (DLs) models. However, they did not consider the full potential of CNNs being deployed on the FPGAs’ PL.

In this work, we explore the potential of FPGAs’ PL to execute ANNs for image classification. We will consider the development board AMD ZCU104 FPGA [11], and using PyTorch/Brevitas [12] and FINN [13], [14], we deployed two CNNs in the PLs of the FPGA. This work aims to find a solution to classify images in real-time.

The main contributions of this work are the release of an open-access dataset RG2C of small tiles (32 px × 32 px) of grapes’ images for classification purposes. This dataset was used to test and deploy a BNN CNV, a 2-bit CNV, and a 4-bit MobileNet. In summary, we claim that: small-size classification models can be used to identify objects into images; the use of the PL is suitable for executing classification ANN; we released a challenging dataset of tiles of images for detection of fruits in images; we can beat the real-time while inferring images using small size ANNs in FPGAs; we can use the FPGA’s PL to deploy ANNs for the attention mechanisms of robotic systems.

This work benchmarks a set of small-sized ANNs models in a tile dataset of images of grapes. So, in this section, we will

explore the required material and the procedures for deploying the ANNs in the FPGA ’s PL.

A. RG2C dataset

Research suggests that small-sized ANN operating on dedicated hardware can significantly accelerate the inference process. The new dataset red grape chunk classification (RG2C) was compiled to investigate this. The RG2C dataset consists of image segments depicting bunches of red grapes in steep-slope vineyards, classified in a binary manner.

These images were captured using a RGB camera at Quinta do Seixo, Valenc¸a do Douro, Portugal, in video format. An operator utilised a smartphone POCO F2 PRO (for details on the characteristics, see [15]) and manually navigated through the vineyards, recording video samples of the canopy with mature grape bunches. All frames were captured as redgreen-blue (RGB) images, allowing for some sequential and repetitive images. The dataset includes 1198 images, each with a resolution of 1920 px × 1080 px.

Subsequently, each image was divided into 32 px × 32 px segments, as illustrated in Figure 1. This segmentation process, performed without overlap, yielded a total of 10 782 images.
Fig. 1: Illustration of the image segmentation scheme for the RG2C dataset.

Supervised learning techniques were applied. A binary classification method was used, classifying the entire image segment as either containing grapes or not, rather than identifying individual grapes within a bounding box. The dataset was organised in an Image Directory structure.

The labelling process was conducted in two phases. Initially, a colour threshold technique was used to sort images into their respective class folders (grape or no_grape), taking advantage of the distinct colour of the red grape bunches against the background. However, some mislabelling occurred, necessitating a manual verification process to correct inaccurately labelled images. An image was classified as belonging to the grape category if it contained at least 25 % of a grape bunch.

Finally, the dataset was split into three sets considering the acquisition sequence of the images: train (60 %), validation (20 %), and test (20 %). The train set contains 6470 images, the validation set 2156 images, and the test set 2156 images.

The RG2C dataset [16] was made publicly available.

B. FINN and Brevitas

FINN [13], [14] is a comprehensive, Docker-based environment provided by AMD. Unlike Vitis-AI [17], FINN operates directly on the PL layer of FPGAs, converting ANNs into Verilog code, register transfer logic (RTL) designs, and intelectual property (IP) blocks. It is a freely available, open-source framework dedicated to constructing, executing, and deploying quantised neural network (QNN) on FPGA platforms. FINN offers a robust suite of tools and modules that streamline the entire QNN development process, from design to deployment, thereby enhancing the efficiency of DL models.

A notable limitation of FINN is its exclusive compatibility with PyTorch, because of Brevitas [12] dependency. Consequently, all network designs must be tailored to this specification. Nonetheless, FINN provides the capability to manipulate and adjust DL models down to the bit level, thereby enabling the optimisation and compression of network operations to this granularity. This is facilitated by Brevitas, a supplementary library to PyTorch, which redefines common ANN operations to allow designers to specify the desired bit precision for computations.

In contrast to the conventional approach of employing a deep learning processing unit (DPU) IP core as an intermediary for DL models between the processing unit (PS) and PL, FINN directly deploys a dedicated IP core for each model. This strategy is primarily constrained by the finite number of available configurable logic blocks, necessitating careful adjustment of network parallelisation settings and adopting compact-sized ANNs for implementation.

C. ANNs architectures

1) CNV: A CNV is structured with sequential layers, including two convolution layers and a maximum pooling layer.

Three sequential dense layers power the network’s prediction head. The design and structure of this proposed network are depicted in the diagram in Figure 3 and detailed in Table I, both implementing the framework originally introduced by [13] for the FINN architecture.

To facilitate the deployment of the CNV on a FPGA, we will explore two variants: one with two-bit operations in each layer and another with single-bit operations per layer. The latter is recognised as a BNN [18], [19]. BNNs are designed to achieve optimal efficiency by converting all operations into binary bitlevel computations, which are more efficiently processed at the logic level.

2) MobileNet v1: MobileNet v1 [5] is a DL model designed for mobile and low-computing devices. In its original implementation, it is designed for classification tasks. The used version of this classifier was implemented in PyTorch as initially stated. However, some changes in the layers were made to ensure that the ANN fits in the FPGA PL and is compatible with input data of 32 × 32 px. At the end of the MobileNet v1 was appended a prediction head composed of an average pooling layer, a fully connected layer and a quantised rectified linear unit (ReLU).

MobileNet v1, as described by [5], is a DL model optimised for mobile and low-resource computing devices. Primarily designed for classification tasks, this model’s architecture has been adapted for efficient implementation.

In the version utilised, the MobileNet v1 model was implemented using PyTorch, in line with the original description. Modifications were made to its layers to ensure that the ANN is suitable for deployment on FPGAs’ PL and to handle input data with a resolution of 32 px × 32 px. To accommodate the deployment requirements, the architecture of MobileNet v1 was appended with a prediction head. This additional component consists of an average pooling layer, a fully connected layer, and a quantised ReLU.

subsection: D. Deploying on the FPGA through FINN
text:
The process of deploying FPGAs using FINN is outlined in a sequential manner, as depicted in the referenced FINN flowchart, Figure 2. The procedure up to the Brevitas export shares similarities with other network deployments and utilises Pytorch. A crucial step involves Brevitas, which is used to implement specific quantisation nodes. These nodes are essential for specifying the bit count for the various operations.

After training, the network is exported to a standard model format known as FINN-ONNX, which is compatible with the open neural network exchange (ONNX) format (a standard for interoperability of machine learning (ML) models between different frameworks [20]). This FINN-ONNX model undergoes several transformations aimed at optimising the network architecture, ensuring it aligns well with AMD-Xilinx IP and the FPGA’s PL. Key operations include streamlining [21], eliminating unnecessary floating-point operations, merging multiple operations into a single one when feasible, and converting some operations into multiple threshold nodes. These adjustments help reduce the number of operations and enhance parallelisation, resulting in a faster network that effectively utilises the FPGA space.

Next, the network is transitioned into High Level Synthesis (HLS) layers, followed by conversion into custom IP modules or a series of IPs. This stage allows for numerous simulations to evaluate the network’s optimisation level. The final step involves translating the IPs into instructions that the FPGA can understand.

Control over the network’s parallelisation is achieved through two parameters: single instruction multiple data (SIMD) and process element (PE). SIMD relates to the number of data elements processed concurrently in a single computation, while PE refers to the number of parallel computations. The optimisation of these parameters must adhere to (1) and (2), to ensure all FPGA space is efficiently used. In both equations, H and W represent the number of input and output features, respectively. These equations follow the congruence relation notation [22] and state that the remainder between the integer division of the two values is zero.

An advantage of this deployment strategy is the direct implementation of ANNs into logic circuits (configurable logic blocks), optimising performance. Additionally, Brevitas enables bit-level control over the networks. For this analysis, three scenarios were considered:

• A MobileNet v1 with four-bit quantised weights and biases (‘mobilenet w4a4’);

• A CNV with two-bit quantised weights and biases (’cnv w2a2’); and

• A CNV with one-bit quantised weights and biases (’cnv w1a1’). This protocol assures a probable optimisation of the deep neural networks under low-power and high-performing devices. However, they may detect multiple objects simultaneously. The following strategies aim to develop algorithms that can filter the different objects.

During this section, we explore the ability of the FPGA to execute ANNs and identify objects into images. This involves deploying ANNs as an FPGA IPs through the FINN framework. We present our results to show the capabilities of our method and to support our main claims, which are that the use of the FPGA’s PL to run a small-sized ANN can be used to identify the objects in classification images from RG2C. Secondly, using the FPGA’s PL can outperform the real-time. Thirdly, the use of small-size ANNs into FPGAs are suitable for fast inference speed for the attention mechanisms of robotic systems.

For the experimental setup, we resorted to the test set from the dataset. After training and deploying the different ANNs, we tested the results against the test set of the dataset. The experimental process was performed at two different levels. Firstly, we assessed the capability of the ANNs to classify the different tiles correctly. From this level, we extract performance metrics. Then, we measure the inference speed from the different ANNs and assess the inference framerate. The second level delivers us the required information to validate the capability of our ANNs to outperform the realtime, i.e. approximately 25 FPS. Both levels aid in validating the suitability of this strategy for applications in the attention mechanisms of robotic perception systems.

subsection: C. Assessing the speed of inference
text:
The inference speed was further evaluated, as detailed in (4). Figure 8 illustrates the frame rate for different models deployed on the FPGA’s PL using the FINN framework. MobileNet v1, with four bits for both weights and biases, achieved speeds up to 263 faster than the FPGA from [10] running at 25 FPS. Conversely, CNV only managed to be 32 faster. Given that CNV is significantly smaller than MobileNet v1, there is

potential for further optimisation and speed improvements for CNV compared to MobileNet v1.

Therefore, the use of the FPGAs’ PL speeds up the execution of DL models in a manner that they become usable for robotics attention mechanisms, acting as an alerting system. At this stage, we can also prove that the use of the FPGA’s PL instead of the DPU deliver advantages, and the ANNs can be sped up to their maximum execution capabilities.

In this article, we explore a strategy to increase the efficiency of executing ANNs into FPGAs by optimising the resources available at the PLs. We could effectively train and deploy the ANNs inside the PL using FINN. Firstly, we designed a tile-type visual dataset containing images of bunches of grapes in the vineyards. We release the dataset in open access in [16]. Then, we trained three different ANNs models for detecting the fruits in the images. We designed the models using Pytorch and the Brevitas library to convert the various layers into their equivalent for quantised weights. A pipeline from FINN is applied to transform and adjust the ANNs to fit inside the available PL. Through this article, we assess the capability to use this ANNs deployed on FPGA’s PL to develop an efficient and fast attention mechanism for robotics perception systems. The models could effectively detect the fruits in the images and outperformed the regular speed of cameras, i.e. approximately 25 FPS.
